lesson: [middlegame] When your piece is attacked and a pawn near your king is loose, defend with a developing move (Nc3, Nbd2, Be3) instead of shuffling the attacked piece Example: Move 14 Bd5 was hit by Nb4; Be4 "defended d3" but Nc3 was far better and kept +87%

[middlegame] Before putting a bishop on a central square, check every enemy pawn that can advance to attack it (d5, f5, e5, c5) and verify a safe retreat exists Example: Be4 met ...d5/...f5; the bishop had no square (Bf5 Qxf5, Bg6 fxg6) and was lost for two pawns

[middlegame] Never swap a bishop or knight for two pawns while pieces are active; first search all checks and sacrifices that win the piece back or expose the king Example: Trapped on e4 I played Bxd5 for pawns; Bxh7+ first was stronger and kept more winning chances

[middlegame] With a clear material edge, play the simplest consolidating developing move; avoid clever maneuvers that put pieces on squares pawns can attack Example: A piece up at 87%, Be4 instead of Nc3 threw away most of the advantage in two moves

[opening] Before any exchange sequence on an open file, recount defenders of your central pawn e4/d4 after the trades Example: 8.a4 axb5 9.axb5 Rxa8 allowed 10...Nxe4 because the rook trade cost e4 its guard

[middlegame] When choosing between recaptures, prefer taking the opponent's most active piece over a greedy pawn grab that lets their piece escape with tempo Example: 19.dxc5 instead of Rxe5 let ...Rd8 and ...Nd3 infiltrate; evaluation fell from 54% to 44%

[middlegame] Deny enemy knights the d3/c2/f3 outposts: control them with a rook, bishop or pawn (c3, Be3) before the knight arrives, not after Example: Black's ...Nd3 repeatedly harassed my rook and queen because no piece covered d3

[middlegame] If two enemy knights attack one pawn defended only by your queen, add a defender with a knight or advance the pawn; a queen-only guard invites Nxd3 removal tactics Example: d3 was hit by Nb4 and Nc5 with just Qd1 guarding, forcing awkward bishop moves

[middlegame] Before every move, list your undefended pieces and the squares where one enemy move can hit two of them; fix the loosest one first Example: Bishop on d5/e4 plus pawn d3 both loose gave Black tempo moves ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5

[middlegame] When your bishop pair is deep in enemy territory on light squares, keep a pawn or knight supporting the outpost, else the bishop is just a target Example: Bd5 and Be4 were both chased by pawns because c4/d3 support never came

[endgame] With an extra pawn and rooks on, activate the rook behind or beside the passer and trade off the opponent's active knight before advancing Example: After c5 my passer went nowhere while Black's knight on d3/b3 tied my pieces down

[endgame] Before simplifying into a pawn-up ending, check the opponent's knight cannot reach a fork square near your rook and king; trade knights if it can Example: Nxc5/Nb3 kept forking ideas alive and nearly equalized a winning position

[middlegame] Convert an attack by looking for back-rank and last-rank rook invasions (R to 8th) once the opponent's pieces drift to one wing Example: 24.Rd8 worked only because Black's knight was on b3 and queen on a6, far from the king
[opening] In the Spanish with Ba4/Bb3, delay flank pawn pushes (a4) until Nc3 or d3/c3 is in and e4 has two defenders Example: 8.a4 came before Nc3/Nbd2 and the resulting trades cost the e4 pawn

[middlegame] Compare candidate moves by asking "what is my opponent's best reply pawn push?" before deciding; if a pawn push gains a tempo on you, pick another move Example: ...d5 and ...f5 both gained tempo on Be4; checking pawn pushes first would have revealed Nc3

[middlegame] Before any queen or piece move, list every enemy PAWN that captures the destination square; a pawn defender refutes any fork or double attack Example: 26...Qc3 forked rooks on a1/d2 but 27.bxc3 simply took the queen for a pawn

[middlegame] When ahead, win material by force (hanging piece, clean pin) rather than by a fork; verify the forking square is attacked by nothing at all Example: At 98% winning, Qc3's "double attack" lost the queen; quiet Qe4 kept everything

[middlegame] Before every move, list your undefended pieces and squares where one enemy move hits two of them; fix the loosest first Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave the opponent free tempo moves ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5

[middlegame] Ask "what is my opponent's best pawn push/capture reply?" for each candidate; if a pawn gains tempo or wins material, pick another move Example: ...d5 and ...f5 chased a bishop with no retreat; bxc3 refuted Qc3

[endgame] With bishop plus pawns versus rook, keep pawns connected and defended by each other or the king; isolated pawns on open lines are eaten one by one Example: 29...dxc4 and 31...c5 left a6/c4/c6 scattered; Rd6-b6-a6 collected them all

[endgame] When choosing a recapture with the enemy rook active, pick the one that keeps your pawn chain linked, even if it concedes a doubled pawn Example: 29...bxc4 kept c6+c4+a6 linked; 29...dxc4 broke the mass and dropped from 50% to 9%

[endgame] Do not let your lone bishop be the only defender of pawns: a rook attacking the bishop forces trade or loss of the whole queenside Example: 33.Rd6/34.Rc6 hit the b6 bishop until Bd6 Rxd6 won it and every pawn after

[endgame] Before your king captures material on the edge, count the pawn race: check your king stays inside the square of all enemy passers Example: 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f4-f5-f6 and h4-h8 promoted two queens unstoppably

[middlegame] Deny enemy knights and rooks the d3/c2/f3/6th-rank entry squares with a pawn or piece before they arrive, not after Example: Opponent's rook reached d6/c6 freely once my pawns no longer covered those squares
